one_liner: Pure-Go WebAssembly MVP interpreter with gas metering; 2018 runs beat the then-current wasmi and wagon by about 2x.
what_it_does: Life loads a WebAssembly MVP module into a Go VirtualMachine (exec.NewVirtualMachine with a VMConfig and an ImportResolver), and you call exported functions by ID with int64 arguments. Host imports come from a resolver interface that returns Go closures. Limits on memory pages, table size, value slots, call depth and gas (a pluggable per-instruction GasPolicy) are built in, because the target was smart contracts. It is not a drop-in replacement for wasmi or wagon: the API is its own, and it has no WASI.
how_it_is_fast: Before execution, each function is translated from the Wasm stack bytecode into an SSA-style register IR (compiler/ssa.go). Registers are then assigned per stack slot. The FIXME in liveness.go says there is no real liveness-based allocation yet. The interpreter runs this register code in one big switch loop over 5-byte instruction headers (uint32 target register plus opcode), which avoids the push/pop traffic of a stack interpreter. The optional Polymerase engine translates the whole module to C, compiles it with clang -O2 -fPIC -shared at run time and dlopens the result through cgo. The 'JIT' timed in the 2018 gist was an earlier engine: it generated C per function, compiled it with cc -O1 and dlopened it, and it has since been removed.
when_to_use: A Go program that must run untrusted Wasm MVP modules with per-instruction gas accounting and hard memory/call-depth caps, without cgo (interpreter-only mode).
Studying or forking a small, readable register-IR Wasm interpreter written in Go (SSA translation plus a switch loop).
Legacy deployments already pinned to Life whose modules are plain integer-heavy MVP code (no SIMD, threads, bulk memory or reference types).
when_not_to_use: Any new project. The repo has had no commit since 2019-12-03, 29 issues are open, and modern Go runtimes (wazero, or the catalogued Go sibling wazy) and modern interpreters (wasm3, Wasmi) are maintained and much faster.
Raw speed. wasm3's docs/Interpreter.md (independent, 4 GHz Core i7 iMac) times Life at 547 s on Mandelbrot vs wasm3 17.9 s, and 153 s on CRC32 vs 5.1 s, roughly 30x slower.
WASI programs, or modules built by current toolchains that emit post-MVP features: neither is supported (issue #96 asks for WASI; issue #112 asks about Go-built Wasm).
Floating-point-heavy code: open issue #98 reports wrong pow() results (pow(3.0, 0.3) gives 1.1293 instead of 1.3904).

Using Polymerase in production: it needs cgo, clang on the host at run time and dlopen of a temp file. The AOTService only invokes functions with 0, 1 or 2 parameters, and open bug #90 reports fib returning 0 with Polymerase enabled.

integration.dependencies: github.com/go-interpreter/wagon v0.6.0 (parser, disassembler, validation), github.com/vmihailenco/msgpack; Polymerase also needs cgo, libdl and a clang binary on PATH at run time
integration.min_toolchain: go.mod says go 1.13 (Go modules required; README uses GO111MODULE=on)
integration.platforms: Interpreter: any Go target (pure Go). Polymerase: aot_unix.go includes runtime_linux_x86_64.h, and there are separate aot_windows.go and aot_android_arm.go files plus a js/wasm placeholder; other platforms print 'not yet supported'.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; a VirtualMachine holds mutable run state (frames, Delegate, InsideExecute, Exited), so use one VM per goroutine

gotchas: Harness flaw: the committed bench/cases/run_item.sh runs '../../life -jit', but current main.go defines no -jit flag (only -entry, -polymerase and -no-fp), and exec/vm.go prints 'Warning: JIT support is removed.'. The script fails at HEAD, and the gist's 'Life (JIT enabled)' columns (1.672 s, 1.072 s, 3.898 s) came from a removed per-function C codegen engine (cc -O1 plus dlopen) that you cannot use today.

Harness flaw: the README chart (media/bench.png, updated 2018-12-17) shows near-zero 'Life (Polymerase)' bars, but no raw numbers or method exist for them, while its interp/wagon/wasmi bars are the August 2018 gist values. The next day (b783dc5, 2018-12-18) snappy_compress was changed to loop 1000 times. The gist's return value 393476 is one compression of 8 MiB of zeros, so the committed workload no longer matches any published number.

Methodology: all numbers are whole-process 'time' real values, so Life's figures include Go startup, validation and SSA compilation, and wasmi's include its own load. The commands used to run wagon and wasmi are not in the repo or the gist. The snappy case compresses an all-zero buffer, a degenerate input dominated by the match-extension loop.

Errors inside the VM are Go panics recovered in Execute and stored in vm.ExitError; open issues #99, #100 and #104 report panic handling, unreachable detection and 'inconsistent stack pattern' failures.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Life only when you are maintaining an existing Life integration that depends on its gas-metering API. For new Go embeddings, use wazy (the catalogued wazero fork) or wasm2go, and for a fast interpreter use wasm3 or Wasmi: all are maintained and beat Life's interpreter by large margins.
verified_claims_summary: In August 2018, the author's gist timed three Rust programs compiled to wasm32-unknown-unknown (128-bit Pollard rho, one Snappy compression of 8 MiB of zeros, fib(35)) with shell 'time'. Life's interpreter took 2.18/2.98/3.07 s against 4.85/7.02/5.81 s for the 2018 wasmi and 4.35/5.44/6.20 s for wagon, about 1.9-2.4x faster than wasmi (derived from page data). The timings state no CPU, Go version or engine versions, and the 'JIT' column comes from an engine that has since been removed.
status_note: Abandoned since December 2019 (not archived) and MIT-licensed. The pure-Go interpreter still builds as a module, but the benchmark script no longer runs against current main.go and the published speedups describe 2018 competitors, so treat it as a historical reference rather than a current fast choice.
